title: 2 Nepal nationals held for murder in Shimla district - The Tribune
description: 2 Nepal nationals held for murder in Shimla district  The Tribune
publisher.title: The Tribune
full_article:
Shimla district police have arrested two Nepal nationals for allegedly murdering a fellow Nepali labourer in the Jubbal area. The accused were apprehended at the Inter-State Bus Terminus (ISBT), Shimla, while allegedly planning to flee to Nepal. title: US Hoteliers Mobilize Aid for Nepal Flood Victims Through AAHOA - Asian Hospitality
description: US Hoteliers Mobilize Aid for Nepal Flood Victims Through AAHOA  Asian Hospitality
publisher.title: Asian Hospitality
full_article:
AS NEPAL CONTINUES to recover from a massive flood in August, U.S. hoteliers are gathering aid to send to the country. The AAHOA Charitable Foundation is organizing the effort to raise funds, donations and volunteers to bring to Nepal in January.

The Aug. 26 flood, triggered by a rock-and-ice avalanche into a Himalayan mountain lake, has so far killed more than 1,400 people with more than 6000 unaccounted for, according to Big News Network. It has left more than 70,000 people homeless.

“It's so sad to see that these lives are just completely washed away, and they had no idea this was happening,” said Lina Patel, director of strategic franchise initiatives for Red Roof and one of the organizers of the ACF efforts. “We took a helicopter there to do a prayer and a puja after three weeks and you cannot tell that there was a civilization there. That whole area is back to its natural state. You cannot even see a pipe or a wire sticking out or anything. Everybody is just buried hundreds of feet under that sand and rock.”

Planning the mission

Patel regularly leads expeditions and pilgrimages in the Himalayas. She is very familiar with the area where the worst of the flood hit.

“That whole valley where villages were, that was the road that connects Nepal to China, and there was a trade route along with the Pilgrims' route, and all these villages thrive based on the trade route and the pilgrims' route,” she said. “Now that route is completely washed away, I believe the government is still deciding on what to do next.”

Fellow AAHOA lifetime members Nayna Patel, Maya Patel and Manisha Patel are serving with Lina as liaisons between ACF and Child Environment Nepal to coordinate delivery of the aid. The women, all of whom have traveled with Lina to Nepal previously, will cover their own travel expenses to visit affected communities, communicate local needs and share updates on approved relief efforts, according to ACF.

Along with cash donations, ACF are collecting staple foods, blankets and essential supplies ahead of winter. It will help fund approved recovery projects, including rebuilding homes and schools, when they go to Nepal in January. They also are looking for volunteers to join them, Lina said.

“Our plan is to go to Nepal sometimes in January to oversee the effort and do a volunteer trip,” Lina said. “We're going to invite whoever would like to come to help us do volunteer there. That way, 100 percent of the funds that are collected goes directly towards the efforts of rebuilding the lives of the families that have lost their members.”

Lina said ACF also reached out to many of the organizations across the country, such as Hindu temples and Leuva Patidar Samaj of USA. They now are collaborating with ACF.

Second mission of mercy

All four women also gathered donations for the construction of a new school in a village hit by a 2015 earthquake that also devastated Nepal. They travelled four times to oversee the project between 2015 and 2018.

“Luckily that school, which is located in this district where the flood happened, it was untouched and it's safe because it was at a much higher ground,” Patel said.

However, the flood completely wiped out a 7-story hotel where Lina and her groups would stay. Moreover, eight members of her team were killed.

“These are experienced climbers, the Sherpas,” Lina said. “There was no time for them to even go above ground.”

In 2025, members of AAHOA gathered aid for victims of the Los Angeles wildfires.

Individuals and organizations interested in supporting the ACF Nepal Relief & Recovery Fund can contribute at https://donorbox.org/acf-nepal-relief-recovery-fund.

title: Pilot supports daily parent-reported illness diaries in Nepal - Bioengineer.org
description: Pilot supports daily parent-reported illness diaries in Nepal  Bioengineer.org
publisher.title: Bioengineer.org
full_article:
Parents in a 12-week pilot study in Nepal completed daily written diaries of common respiratory and diarrheal symptoms for children under five at high rates, supporting the feasibility of using the method in a larger longitudinal investigation. Across 672 child-weeks of data collection, 98.5% included at least one completed diary day and 88.7% were completed for all seven days. The study involved 56 children in 40 households in the Western Chitwan Valley. Weekly telephone interviews took an average of 5.9 minutes and created an opportunity to obtain information when a diary had not been filled in every day. The findings concern completion and feasibility rather than the diagnostic accuracy of parent-reported symptoms or the health effects of the method.

The pilot was designed to test a high-frequency symptom-reporting approach that could later be combined with the Chitwan Valley Family Study, a longitudinal household and community panel that has collected detailed information about children, parents, households, and communities since 1996. Researchers randomly selected households with children under five from within the family study’s geographic area but outside its established sample neighborhoods, avoiding contamination of the samples planned for the follow-on investigation. Sampling was stratified by the number of age-eligible children, with about half of the households having one child under five and about half having two. Half of the households were then randomized to receive a daily text-message reminder, with this randomization also stratified by the number of eligible children.

All respondents were mothers of children under five. Trained interviewers visited the selected households, confirmed that the children met the age requirement, obtained informed consent, and explained the symptom definitions using the diary’s written instructions and pictures. Diarrhea, for example, was defined as three or more loose stools in a 24-hour period. Each paper diary contained seven daily checklists for recording diarrhea, fever, cough, runny nose, fast or labored breathing, loss of appetite, and fatigue. The paper format was intended to make the daily observations easier for parents to record without requiring a visit or telephone contact for every day of the study period.

During the 12-week study, a trained interviewer called each participating mother every week. The interview was designed to take less than 10 minutes and used a computer-assisted personal-interview procedure. Interviewers asked which symptoms the children had experienced and on which days they had occurred. When a respondent had not recorded symptoms in the diary, the interview provided an opportunity to report them from memory. Interviewers also recorded whether the information had come from the completed checklist, recall, or a combination of both, making it possible to distinguish information documented at the time from information supplied later. The final weekly interview included questions about respondents’ experiences with the study.

A diary week was classified as complete only when all days contained complete data for all enrolled children in the household. The participants’ children averaged 26.9 months of age, with a standard deviation of 15.5 months, and 51.8% were female. The proportion of fully completed diary weeks ranged from 87.5% to 94.6% across the study weeks, apart from the first and last weeks, when completion was 67.9% and 80.3%, respectively. The study therefore recorded lower full-week completion at both ends of the observation period, although the results do not identify a cause for those differences.

Mixed-effects logistic regression was used to assess how diary completion varied by week while accounting for clustering at the respondent, or mother, level. The unadjusted model evaluated completion by collection week. A fuller model additionally accounted for collection week, child sex, child age in years, and whether the mother had one or two children enrolled in the study. The investigators reported odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals and p-values. They also used cumulative incidence curves and kernel-density plots to estimate the incidence and prevalence of reported symptoms, and summarized the qualitative feedback collected at the end of the study.

Daily text reminders did not show a statistically significant association with completion. Mothers who received reminders completed 86.3% of diaries fully, compared with 91.3% among those who did not receive texts. The regression estimated the odds of completion at 1.19 for households receiving reminders, but the 95% confidence interval was wide, from 0.31 to 4.53, indicating substantial uncertainty. The pilot therefore did not establish a benefit or disadvantage associated with receiving reminders. It also did not demonstrate that the messages changed the number or type of symptoms reported. Nevertheless, all respondents who had received a text described it as helpful, while 73.7% of those who had not received one said they would prefer to have it.

Runny nose and cough had the highest reported incidence and overall prevalence, whereas fatigue and difficulty breathing were reported least often. The investigators said the pattern of symptom frequency was consistent with their expectations for the season in which data were collected. They also suggested that more common symptoms being reported more often indicated that respondents had understood the study definitions. These observations concern what parents recorded during a single collection period; they do not establish a geographic contrast or demonstrate a change in childhood illness over time. The pilot did not use a diagnostic instrument or clinical or laboratory confirmation to evaluate whether individual entries represented infectious disease.

Respondents said that both the text messages and storing the diary in a visible place helped them remember to complete it each day. They requested a smaller diary and a format that would be easier to store and clearer to complete. The pilot therefore informed several changes for the larger study within the Chitwan Valley Family Study: advising participants about possible storage locations, redesigning the diary, and modifying the protocol so that household caregivers other than the enrolled mother could help complete the written records. Although the pilot found no clear effect of reminders on completion, the favorable feedback led the team to offer daily text messages to all participants in the larger study.

The results support daily parent-reported symptom diaries as a potentially practical way to measure acute childhood illness, but several limitations constrain how broadly the findings can be generalized. The sample included only 40 households and 56 children, and symptom reporting covered 12 weeks, compared with 52 weeks in the larger planned study. The children came from one geographic area and may not represent the wider pediatric population of Chitwan or the full family-study sample. Seasonality also influenced the illnesses reported during the collection period. Longer participation could increase attrition, while selection effects and social desirability might affect diary completion or the information parents provide. The authors proposed cross-checking diaries against respondent-reported data in the follow-on study as one way to identify possible discrepancies.

Within those bounds, the pilot provides evidence that parents are willing to record daily symptoms and that the written diaries can be completed at high rates over a 12-week period. A daily record preserves the timing and frequency of respiratory and diarrheal symptoms, while the brief weekly interview provides a structured opportunity to fill gaps through recall and documents how each report was obtained. When combined with existing social, demographic, household, and community information from the Chitwan Valley Family Study, these data could support analysis of the contextual factors associated with acute illness in early childhood. The study did not demonstrate clinical benefits, improved child health outcomes, or the diagnostic accuracy of the diaries. Its immediate contribution was to identify a workable, relatively low-cost data-collection strategy and refine it for a larger study in Nepal, with possible application in other low- and middle-income countries.

"We had no TV cameras with us since no field equipment was required for the event. All I had was my phone, as did my cameraperson. As the rains intensified, the army barricading the turn to Nuwakot indicated that the tragedy was perhaps bigger than what we anticipated," she wrote in a blog on NDTV.com.

"Even so, NDTV was the first foreign media to be on ground zero in Nepal on August 26. Drenched and with our phones alerting us that water had entered the devices, we continued reporting until late into the night at Nuwakot," she added.

During her extensive coverage, she showed the world the true extent of the tragedy.

She also reported back from Nepal the damage the calamity had wreaked.

"We decided to move and trek to the dead end of the Nepal-Tibet road, which led to Syaphrubesi, then Timure Bazaar, and then the Tibet border. At the dead end was the Chilime hydro project tunnel, where we could see rescue workers and disaster management officials working relentlessly to open the tunnel. We saw helicopters getting the equipment and generators down," she reported.

Scientists have said climate change played a significant role in the Nepal disaster.

Jorge Moreira da Silva, executive director of the UN Office for Project Services (UNOPS), told the news agency AFP that low-carbon-emitting nations shouldn't bear the brunt of climate change.

full_article:
The death toll: What is confirmed, and what remains unknown?

Entire tourism corridors destroyed

Is the rest of Nepal safe for tourism?

Tourism outlook: Recovery will be uneven

What Nepal is doing—and what still needs to change

A second disaster Nepal cannot afford: Lost visitor confidence

 Read this article in your language             Access eTurboNews in 103 languages. Choose your language →

The August 26 catastrophe devastated Himalayan communities, disrupted international pilgrimage and trekking routes, and raised urgent questions about the future of tourism safety in Nepal.

The Nepal–Tibet border flood of August 26, 2026, has become one of the most devastating disasters in Nepal’s recent history. Nearly two months later, thousands remain missing, families are still awaiting identification of victims, and critical roads, bridges, hotels and hydropower facilities have been destroyed.

For Nepal’s tourism industry, the disaster presents two very different realities: devastated mountain destinations facing prolonged disruption, and major tourism centers elsewhere in the country continuing to welcome international visitors.

The central question is no longer simply when tourism will recover. It is whether Nepal can rebuild Himalayan tourism infrastructure to withstand increasingly complex natural disasters—and restore international confidence without minimizing the risks.

When Everest Melts, Who Gets the Bill? Nepal Tourism Faces a Climate Reckoning

The death toll: What is confirmed, and what remains unknown?

REPORTED HUMAN IMPACT — NEPAL 1,410 Reported deaths in September’s NDRRMA update 6,145 Reported missing, September 17 636 Foreign nationals listed missing in September 20 update 13,784 People rescued by September 20 Data note: Figures are dated snapshots, not one reconciled final tally. The Nepal Red Cross reported 1,410 deaths and 6,145 missing in its October situation update; government figures have subsequently been revised.

Entire tourism corridors destroyed

The catastrophe began when a high-altitude mass movement involving rock and ice developed into a destructive debris flow and flash flood. The torrent swept through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems, damaging communities and infrastructure across multiple districts.

According to the World Bank, more than 55 kilometers of the 82-kilometer Galchhi–Rasuwagadhi trade corridor were damaged, including approximately 40 kilometers completely washed away. Thirty-seven motorable bridges and 68 suspension bridges were destroyed or damaged.

Twelve hydropower projects were affected, and more than 200 hotels and restaurants suffered damage.

The tourism consequences are especially serious for Langtang trekking, the sacred Gosaikunda lakes and the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage route. These destinations depend on mountain roads, guides, guesthouses, transport operators and seasonal visitor spending.

A damaged road can therefore eliminate income for an entire tourism community, even when its hotels survive.

Is the rest of Nepal safe for tourism?

The geographical distinction is crucial.

Nepal Tourism Board | National Tourism Organization of Nepal Discover Nepal’s beauty and culture through the Nepal Tourism Board. Your complete resource for accommodation, events, activities, and vacation preparation.

The Pacific Asia Travel Association reported that Kathmandu Valley, Pokhara, the Everest and Annapurna regions, Chitwan, Bardiya and Lumbini were operating normally in its post-disaster travel assessment.

The Langtang–Rasuwa–Bhote Koshi corridor, however, was identified as disrupted and unsuitable for normal tourism operations.

This does not mean every unaffected destination is free from seasonal hazards. Indeed, additional flooding in Gorkha in October stranded more than 100 foreign trekkers, demonstrating that the broader Himalayan risk has not disappeared.

Nepal’s challenge is communicating accurate, destination-specific safety information rather than allowing images from one disaster corridor to define the entire country.

Tourism outlook: Recovery will be uneven

The World Bank expects Nepal’s economic growth to slow to 3.7% in fiscal year 2027, with recovery toward 5.2% in FY2028 as reconstruction advances. Tourism is among the sectors expected to suffer from infrastructure disruption and negative perceptions of travel safety.

The timing is particularly damaging. The August flood struck immediately before Nepal’s September–November autumn tourism season, when trekking operators, hotels and mountain communities typically depend on increased visitor activity.

For Kathmandu, Pokhara and established trekking areas outside the affected corridor, tourism can continue generating income. For Rasuwa’s smaller operators, the loss of access may mean an extended period without viable business.

A nationwide collapse in visitor arrivals cannot be concluded from the available evidence. Verified post-flood arrival and cancellation data would be necessary to calculate the full tourism revenue impact.

What Nepal is doing—and what still needs to change

Nepal has mobilized military and civilian rescue teams, helicopters, engineers and international assistance. Authorities have worked to restore roads, electricity and communications, while displaced households are receiving relief and temporary accommodation support.

The World Bank has made up to $170 million in emergency financing available. Government measures also include requests for local tax and fee concessions for flood-damaged businesses.

The government is also examining safer resettlement, including identifying areas where rebuilding homes may expose residents to repeated disasters.

But tourism protection requires more than reconstruction.

Nepal needs reliable early-warning systems, stronger monitoring of unstable glaciers and mountain slopes, alternative access roads, evacuation procedures for trekkers and pilgrims, and better coordination between tourism operators and emergency authorities.

Scientists warn that temporary river blockages, unstable slopes and secondary debris flows remain serious risks even after the initial floodwaters recede.

These measures must also address cross-border information sharing with China, because hazards originating in remote mountain terrain can move downstream faster than communities can respond.

A second disaster Nepal cannot afford: Lost visitor confidence

For Nepal, the danger is that physical destruction becomes a prolonged economic crisis.

International travelers need clear guidance about which destinations are accessible. Tour operators need dependable transport and emergency communications. Small guesthouse owners need financing and sufficient confidence to reopen.

Promotional campaigns alone cannot resolve these issues.

The flood has exposed a structural vulnerability in Himalayan tourism: too much local economic activity depends on infrastructure concentrated in narrow valleys exposed to multiple natural hazards.

Nepal’s recovery will ultimately be measured not simply by rebuilt bridges or renewed visitor arrivals, but by whether residents, tourism workers and international visitors are better protected when the next disaster strikes.

The country remains an important international tourism destination. Its future competitiveness, however, will increasingly depend on making safety and resilience as central to its tourism identity as its extraordinary Himalayan landscapes.

Nepal Landslide Energy Matched 3.5-Magnitude Quake

KATHMANDU – A massive landslide in Nepal’s Gorkha district on October 11 triggered repeated flood surges in the Budhi Gandaki River, releasing energy comparable to that of a magnitude-3.5 earthquake, according to a preliminary assessment by the Department of Mines and Geology.

The landslide occurred in the upper reaches of the Ungdilung Khola, a tributary of the Budhi Gandaki River. Snow, water and debris swept down the mountainside, blocking river channels and triggering successive surges when the accumulated material and water broke through, the report said.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), citing the assessment, said the largest surge reached an estimated height of 20 to 25 meters. At least five people were reported missing, while several hydropower projects, roads and bridges were damaged or destroyed.

The incident occurred between Chamar Himal and Syerangi Himal, in Chumnubri Rural Municipality near the Chinese border.

According to the report, an avalanche originated at an altitude of about 6,000 meters in the Tibetan Tethys Himalaya, where rock formations are relatively weak. A landslide followed at around 5,500 meters, sending snow, water and debris south along the Ungdilung Khola.

The debris accumulated at the narrow confluence of the Ungdilung Khola and Syar Khola, another tributary of the Budhi Gandaki River, at an altitude of around 2,000 meters. Repeated blockages and releases of water and debris likely generated successive surges, with the large volume of material carried downstream contributing significantly to the biggest flood.

The first mud-laden surge reached the Salleri area, where a camp for the 341-MW Budhi Gandaki Hydroelectric Project was located. The largest surge arrived at around 6:30 a.m., reaching an estimated height of 20 to 25 meters and sweeping away the camp, the report said.

The surge caused major damage downstream, particularly in the Jagat area along the Budhi Gandaki River, where several buildings were affected. Permanent bridges over the Soti Khola and the Budhi Gandaki River were also damaged.

Field observations indicated that the Syar Khola had stopped flowing about an hour before the largest surge arrived. Water had accumulated over a stretch of around 1.5 kilometers in the river’s upper reaches, the report said. Smaller surges continued after the largest one had passed.

The October 11 disaster was the second major flooding event in roughly six weeks, following floods along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers on August 26 that caused extensive damage to communities, hydropower facilities, roads and bridges. (IANS)

Nepal-based Community Homestay Network (CHN) is calling on Australian travel advisors who specialise in immersive, conscious and culture-led travel to apply for its Upper Mustang Nepal famil with limited spaces available and applications closing on 30 October 2026.

Ground costs for the 12-day December 2026 Nepal famil are included, but advisors will need to cover their own flights to the country.

The invitation was first issued in August, then paused after devastating floods hit Nepal. CHN has reopened the call as Nepal looks to tourism to help communities recover during the peak season.

Where does the Nepal famil go?

The view from the multi-storey Sky Caves near Chhoser village in the Upper Mustang region of Nepal.

The Upper Mustang Overland Tour: 12-day Trans-Himalayan Community Experience trip heads into Upper Mustang, a remote Trans-Himalayan region accessible overland by 4WD along the ancient trade route that once connected Nepal and Tibet.

The 12-day Nepal famil itinerary starts in Kathmandu with the Tibetan Buddhist practice of Boudha Kora (walking in a clockwise direction around the historic Boudhanath Stupa) and a welcome dinner, then moves through the Annapurna foothills before reaching the wind-carved cliffs and canyons of Mustang.

Hotel room in Kathmandu – part of the 12-day Nepal famil open to Australian travel advisors.

Advisors will stay with local families in villages, including Narchyang, Kagbeni, Lubra, Hemjakot and Kagbeni, explore the Sky Caves of Chhoser and walk the streets of Lo Manthang, the walled capital of the former Kingdom of Lo.

A night in Lubra brings the group into one of the last active Bon settlements in Nepal, a tradition older than Buddhism in the region. The journey closes with a descent through the Kali Gandaki valley to Pokhara and a return to Kathmandu, finishing with a sound healing session.

How do advisors get there?

The ancient Buddhist Niphu Cave Monastery built into the side of a cliff in the remote Upper Mustang region of Nepal.

CHN Founder Shiva Dhakal said air access to Nepal has improved through multiple regional hubs with Thai Airways, Singapore Airlines, Cathay Pacific, Sichuan Airlines, SriLankan Airlines and Indian carriers, including Air India, connecting Australians through key Asian gateways.

A traditional Tibetan Buddhist chorten (stupa) in Lo Manthang, the walled capital of the Upper Mustang region in Nepal.

“Travelling with Community Homestay Network means seeing a different side of Nepal in a way that supports and empowers local people in lesser-known parts of the country. We already know Aussie travellers love this style of tourism, so we’re excited to open their minds to a new region of the country,” Dhakal said.

“Nepal has become more accessible with improved air connectivity via multiple regional hubs. There’s never been a better time to tick off this bucket-list destination in a new way.”

What can advisors sell after the Nepal famil?

Lopa men in Lo Manthang with prayer beads and hand-held prayer wheels.

CHN works with 51 communities across Nepal and offers 51 bookable experiences, including 41 community homestays and 10 artisan-focused experiences.

The social enterprise has also introduced its first fixed-departure trips for advisors to sell with eight multi-day itineraries on guaranteed departures. More than 100 multi-day departures are now bookable for travel through to December 2027.

Experiences can be sold directly by advisors with on-the-ground knowledge and logistical support provided by the Nepal-based team.

KARRYON UNPACKS: Upper Mustang is fresh territory for most Australian advisors and a fam that covers ground costs is a low-barrier way to build firsthand knowledge of a remote, community-led product. With Nepal leaning on tourism after the August 2026 floods, the trip doubles as a chance to sell a part of the Himalaya few clients have heard of and support recovery.

title: Low-Dose Nivolumab Shows Responses in Retrospective Nepal Cancer Cohort - Bioengineer.org
description: Low-Dose Nivolumab Shows Responses in Retrospective Nepal Cancer Cohort  Bioengineer.org
publisher.title: Bioengineer.org
full_article:
In a retrospective study of 31 patients with advanced cancers treated at a single center in Nepal, low-dose nivolumab was associated with an overall response rate of 51.6% and a disease control rate of 67.7%. The cohort received 20 or 40 milligrams every three weeks after showing limited response to conventional treatment and being unable to afford the standard regimen. Sixteen of the 31 patients, or 51.6%, achieved a complete or partial response, while five had stable disease.

These observations suggest clinical activity across several tumor types, but the small, uncontrolled cohort, heterogeneous treatments and limited follow-up prevent firm conclusions about the effectiveness of reduced doses relative to standard dosing. Researchers analyzed patients treated between March 2022 and March 2024. The population included gastrointestinal, lung, head-and-neck, gynecologic, skin cancers and Hodgkin lymphoma.

The median age was 51 years, with a range of 28 to 87 years. Eleven patients had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 and 12 had a status of 1, while five had a status of 2 and three had a status of 3. Eight patients, representing 25.8% of the cohort, received nivolumab without previous systemic therapy; the others had received one or more prior lines of treatment.

Five patients also received cytotoxic chemotherapy alongside nivolumab, introducing heterogeneity that complicates attribution of responses or other outcomes to the reduced-dose antibody alone. Investigators selected either a 20- or 40-milligram dose according to the treating physician’s preference and the patient’s financial circumstances. The 20-milligram dose was administered to 20 patients, or 64.5% of the cohort, while 11 patients, or 35.5%, received 40 milligrams.

Patients were explicitly informed that nivolumab was being used off label at a reduced dose and that the supporting evidence was limited. Because the hospital pharmacy stocked nivolumab in 40-milligram vials, the pharmacy implemented vial sharing. Treatment continued until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity or financial hardship prevented further therapy.

Patients who received only one dose or whose records were incomplete were excluded from the analysis. Response was evaluated using the available radiological imaging, which included ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging or positron-emission tomography combined with computed tomography. Solid-tumor responses were assessed under Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1, while the patient with Hodgkin lymphoma was assessed under the Lugano classification.

Progression was recorded only when imaging showed unequivocal tumor enlargement or the appearance of new lesions consistent with malignant progression. Adverse events documented in routine medical records were retrospectively abstracted and graded with version 5.0 of the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events. Grade 1 events were not systematically recorded during outpatient visits, so the safety analysis was restricted to reliably documented events.

Patients received a median of nine nivolumab cycles, with a range of two to 20, over a median treatment duration of 5.7 months, ranging from 0.7 to 17.1 months. The best documented response was a complete response in four patients, or 12.9%, and a partial response in 12, or 38.7%. Stable disease occurred in five patients, or 16.1%; seven patients had progressive disease, and three were not evaluated for their best response.

Among all 31 patients, the overall response rate was 51.6%, with a 95% confidence interval of 33.1% to 69.8%, and the disease control rate was 67.7%, with a 95% confidence interval of 48.6% to 83.3%. Among the 28 evaluable patients, the corresponding rates were 57.1% and 75%, with 95% confidence intervals of 37.2% to 75.5% and 55.1% to 89.3%, respectively. Median follow-up was 8.6 months, with a 95% confidence interval of 7.1 to 12.9 months.

Median progression-free survival, measured from the first nivolumab administration until progression or death from any cause, was 8.8 months, with a 95% confidence interval of 6.6 months to not reached. The estimated six-month progression-free survival rate was 66.1%, with a 95% confidence interval of 50.9% to 80.9%. Median overall survival was 14.8 months, with a 95% confidence interval of 11.1 months to not reached.

The median duration of response among patients who achieved a complete or partial response was four months, with a range of 0.8 to 8.2 months. At the end of the study period, three patients were alive without disease, 22 were alive with disease and six had died. Grade 2 or 3 adverse events were uncommon in the available records.

Two patients developed arthralgia, one at grade 2 and one at grade 3. Two patients had grade 2 diarrhea, and one had a grade 2 pericardial effusion. No additional grade 2 or higher events were documented, and no grade 4 events were recorded.

The recorded safety signal was therefore limited, although incomplete capture of grade 1 events, the retrospective design and short follow-up mean that the findings cannot establish that reduced doses have the same safety profile as standard treatment. Financial hardship remained a problem even under the lower-cost regimen: four patients stopped treatment, including one in complete remission and one with a partial response. The results were broadly consistent with several earlier studies discussed by the researchers.

One report found comparable disease control among low, weight-based and conventional doses of immune checkpoint inhibitors across various cancers, while another reported similar response rates with 40-milligram and conventional-dose nivolumab in advanced cancers. In nonsmall-cell lung cancer, a study found no significant difference in response rate, progression-free survival or overall survival between low doses of 20 or 100 milligrams and standard-dose nivolumab. Another study in hepatocellular carcinoma reported no statistical difference in disease control between 20 and 100 milligrams.

A phase III trial across various tumors reported a median overall survival of 5.88 months with 20-milligram nivolumab compared with 4.7 months for standard chemotherapy, along with one-year survival rates of 27.3% and 16.9%, respectively. Another study in head-and-neck cancer reported improved one-year overall survival with 20-milligram nivolumab compared with standard chemotherapy. These are indirect comparisons because the present study involved neither randomized allocation nor a standard-dose nivolumab control group.

Economically, the study regimen used 20 to 40 milligrams every three weeks, compared with approved nivolumab schedules of 240 milligrams every two weeks or 480 milligrams every four weeks. At a reported cost of approximately 7 dollars per milligram, investigators estimated savings of 80% to 90% relative to standard dosing. Vial sharing was used to make use of partially filled vials, and the availability of biosimilar nivolumab was described as another means of reducing treatment costs.

The researchers also cited pharmacokinetic findings suggesting that therapeutic drug monitoring could help investigate more individualized doses, schedules or frequencies, given nivolumab’s reported half-life of about 25 days. Such cost estimates and exposure measurements do not establish therapeutic equivalence: the present cohort lacked a randomized comparison with approved dosing, and clinical responses observed alongside lower expenditure cannot show that reduced doses produce the same benefit. It was retrospective, conducted at one cancer center and included only 31 patients without a control group.

Selection bias is possible because treatment was chosen in the context of each patient’s finances and the treating physician’s preferences. The cancer types, prior treatment histories and performance statuses varied, five patients received concomitant chemotherapy, PD-L1 status was known for only six patients and three were not evaluable for response. Follow-up was too short to characterize long-term durability, late toxicity or survival reliably.

The findings are therefore hypothesis-generating rather than evidence that 20- or 40-milligram nivolumab can replace approved regimens. Larger controlled studies are needed to confirm whether lower doses can reproduce response and survival outcomes, define an appropriate dose range and establish safety more precisely.

title: After Nepal’s recent disaster, it wants to test whether COP31 can deliver climate justice - The Kathmandu Post
description: After Nepal’s recent disaster, it wants to test whether COP31 can deliver climate justice  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
When Urika Tamang last spoke to her husband, he told her he would be home on October 1. A teacher at a government school in Timure, near Nepal’s border with Tibet, he had spent the last eight years living apart from his wife and son so their child could attend a school in Kathmandu.

Tamang, 37, learned that her husband had been killed in the Rasuwa disaster when the school principal, who had been airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment, broke the news to her.

“I told our son, but he still thinks his father will come home for Dashain,” Tamang said. “He did not see his body, so it was difficult for him to believe he had died.”

Now Tamang is trying to find a way to pay for her husband’s Ghewa, a Tamang ritual to help the deceased transition to the afterlife.

“I couldn’t do anything for my husband,” she said. “All I can do now is make sure his Ghewa is done well. But the rituals are expensive.”

Tamang’s loss is part of a much larger reckoning. The Rasuwa disaster on August 26 left 1,455 people dead, nearly 7,000 injured and 5,285 unaccounted for. It swept away infrastructure, hydropower plants and entire towns, with Nepal facing an estimated $4.7 billion in recovery and reconstruction needs. Seven weeks later, as the country prepares for the Conference of the Parties (COP31), the annual meeting of countries that have joined the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), in Turkey next month, families are still grappling with the consequences. Nepal’s struggle to secure timely international support raises a wider question at the heart of climate justice: what does global solidarity mean when money pledged to vulnerable countries is slow to arrive, insufficient for their needs, or offered as loans?

Nepal has appealed to the UN’s Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) for an exceptional, rapid response. The appeal could test whether an international mechanism created to help countries cope with the irreversible impacts of climate change can deliver when disaster-hit communities need it most.

“Rapid response was one of the fundamental purposes for which the Fund was created,” said Maheshwar Dhakal, an alternate member of the FRLD board who also serves as the chief of Climate Change Management Division at Nepal’s Ministry of Forests and Environment. “So far, however, it has not been effective in fulfilling that purpose.”

Nepal has not requested a specific amount for its emergency appeal, Dhakal added. The $20 million cited in some media reports, he clarified, is the budget ceiling under the FRLD’s inaugural call for funding requests through the Barbados Implementation Modalities (BIM), not the amount Nepal had requested after the Rasuwa disaster.



“Even if we receive just twenty rupees, what we want to do is set a precedent for future disasters,” he said. “It would demonstrate to countries that have pledged money that the Fund is necessary and push it to become more effective and give hope to other [climate] vulnerable least developed countries (LDCs) as well.”



Any country can appeal to the Fund for disasters caused by the changing climate, as long as it is a party to the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement. The Fund prioritises least developed countries and small island developing states. Studies linking the disaster to climate change, such as the recent World Weather Attribution analysis of Nepal’s floods, can help strengthen requests for support.



Manjeet Dhakal, an author of the study and an advisor to the Chair of the LDC group on climate change, said that right before Langtang Lirung collapsed, triggering a rock-ice avalanche that turned it into a debris flood, the region had “unusually warm conditions”. July and August 2026 were the warmest months of the year, warming faster than the entire planet.



But even a strong case for support faces a fundamental problem: the Fund itself is dependent on voluntary contributions and has far less money than developing countries need. In its inaugural funding round, 119 developing countries submitted requests worth $2.8 billion, while the Fund had only $342 million available — enough to meet just 12 percent of the requests.



Nepal also submitted three proposals under the Fund’s regular funding window. One from the Alternative Energy Promotion Center , covering projects in “Illam, Kathmandu, and Kavre”, has “reached the final stage of evaluation,” according to Maheshwar Dhakal. The Fund is yet to decide on which of the 176 proposals it will support.

Since it was set up in 2022, the Fund has not released a dollar to any country, despite provisions for rapid response.

“This is challenging because such a request had not come [to FRLD] before, but we have been making good progress,” Manjeet Dhakal said. “We will likely get a positive decision very soon.”

He added that the Fund would first allocate the money, after which Nepal would have to propose how it would be used before disbursement. The money may come too late for families such as Tamang’s. But how the Fund responds could determine whether families affected by future disasters will wait years, months, or days for support.



The urgency is especially stark right now; it took just seven minutes for the Rasuwa disaster to devastate settlements downstream, yet a Green Climate Fund project to reduce glacier-related flood risks in Nepal took more than seven years to reach implementation.



At the moment, there is no mechanism in the UN through which countries like Nepal, which contribute little to global warming, can demand compensation from the world’s largest carbon emitters whose actions have contributed to the catastrophic damage that will impact generations to come.

For families already struggling to recover, domestic relief may be the quickest source of help.



Truong Huyen-Chi (Shachi), director of the Asia Coordination Office for the Asian Mountain Academic Alliance, said in an email interview that Nepal's own budget and disaster funds are the channels most capable of moving money within days.

Nepal’s prime minister disaster relief fund has collected over Rs. 17.75 billion ($29.75 million). Yet, as the disaster’s 49th day approached, grieving families said they had received no financial assistance from the government.



“In three days, it is the day for Ghewa. But the government has not given the grieving families any money,” said Wanju Wayba Tamang, who has been supporting affected communities.



“If you look at social media, it feels like the government is doing a great job. But on the ground, the government hasn’t returned to check if there is food or anything else that people need. We’ve been going on with the help of individuals and organisations.”



While disasters affect everyone, not everyone has the same resources to recover . Lawyer and social activist Arnab Chaudhary called on the state to acknowledge the disproportionate impact on marginalised communities.



“Even now the state does not have disaggregated data on people living in holding centres. How will it ensure their needs are met?” Chaudhary asked.



Wanju Wayba Tamang is worried about 51 children from Hakubesi, a hamlet in Rasuwa, who have been relocated to Kathmandu. If the state had supported them, they would not have been forced to seek shelter elsewhere, he said, worried about their vulnerability to human trafficking .

The disaster has also renewed questions about the risks communities face when infrastructure is built in fragile mountain environments.

“My brothers gave their lives inside the tunnels while Kathmandu lit bright. It’s not just the World Bank that killed my brothers; it’s the state of Nepal as well,” Wayba Tamang said. “Why did it approve 16 hydropower projects in one corridor? It was like an ambush for my Tamang brothers, on whose sacred lands the state built the plants.”

Civil society groups have also raised concerns about hydropower development and climate risks. In a letter calling on the World Bank Group to halt financing large hydropower projects pending independent risk assessment, over 100 organisations from Nepal and around the globe warned that international financiers had backed hydropower projects despite early warnings about extreme climate risks. They pointed to Upper Trishuli-1, financed by a consortium including the International Finance Corporation (IFC), which they said went ahead despite warnings from as early as 2017.

Severe floods in 2024 and GLOF in 2025 damaged more than 20 hydropower plants, according to the letter sent to the World Bank. Nepal’s energy sector now accounts for 54 percent of its post-disaster recovery budget.

Rebuilding infrastructure raises a further question: who should pay for the additional costs of making it resilient to climate change?

Nepal is already relying heavily on loans to finance climate-related development. A recent Himal Khabar analysis found that over the last decade, for every $1 that Nepal received in grants for climate-related projects through the government’s budget, it took on more than $6 in loans. Nepal’s public debt burden already exceeds $700 per person.



Yet, just 28 days after the Rasuwa disaster, the World Bank offered $170 million to Nepal as an additional loan.

Pakistan’s experience after the devastating floods of 2022, which caused an estimated $30 billion in damage, offers a warning. Much of the international funding offered to Pakistan came as loans rather than grants.



“The international community must ensure that what they did to Pakistan they do not do to Nepal,” Zain Moulvi, director of research at Alternative Law Collective of Pakistan that works in environmental laws, climate finance, and just transition, told Kantipur in a phone interview.



“Developing countries pay three times. First when disasters cause damage. Then because aid is decreasing, they are given loans. Then the government goes through a cycle of austerity, and as disasters recur year after year, the money that is supposed to go to health, education is cut to repay the debt,” said Sunil Acharya, global lead for just transition at the not-for-profit organisation Resource.

For Shachi, climate justice means more than international pledges.

“A widow’s claim should be settled within weeks, children should be kept in school, and recovery assistance should follow people where they now live,” she said. “It would also mean the families are asked what they need, not only counted.”

In his UN speech, Prime Minister Balendra Shah argued that vulnerable countries should not have to borrow to rebuild after disasters they have done little to cause.

“When a climate-driven disaster destroys the infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega loan or patchwork of small grants,” Shah said . “We need adequate grant-based support from the world.”

At COP31 next month, Nepal will have to press for more than financial pledges. It will need to seek accessible loss-and-damage finance, predictable support that does not add to its debt, and mechanisms capable of responding quickly when disasters strike. The US withdrawal from the Paris Agreement has added pressure on the countries that remain committed to climate action, while traditional donors are increasingly directing resources towards defence, conflict and domestic priorities.



“If COP is able to decide to decrease the use of fossil fuels and decrease the rise in global temperature, it would be the greatest achievement for Nepal,” said Manjeet Dhakal. “It would be a win if COP can address a simple way for countries like Nepal to get climate finance.”

Shachi pointed to Barbados as an example of what countries could achieve beyond financial pledges. “Barbados did not win a big number,” she said. “It won a rule: the World Bank now pauses loan repayments for small states hit by disaster. Extending such clauses to mountain countries and LDCs would do more for Nepal over time than any single pledge.”

For Urika Tamang, however, the loss is already irreversible.

title: All that jazz in Nepal - Nepali Times
description: All that jazz in Nepal  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
Jazz was a strange, foreign musical genre in Nepal before Cadenza came along nearly 30 years ago. But this pioneering Nepali jazz-fusion band did not build its following overnight.

Navin Chhetri, drummer and lead singer of Cadenza began jamming with bandmates every Saturday when the Jazz Upstairs Bar opened in Thamel in 1998.

“Cadenza was a hungry band, and we were always looking for new ways to zhuzh up our style,” Chhetri told Nepali Times. “Quickly, we became fascinated with musical improvisation.”

A cadenza is an improvisatory passage in Western classical music, and improvisation has always been the core technique of the band, hence its name. “Rock music was our favourite. We loved jamming to rock bands like Thin Lizzy and the Allman Brothers,” Chhetri recalls.

In the early years, Cadenza drew inspiration from bands like Spin Doctors and Jamiroquai. The band experimented with reggae, then rock and funk, and ultimately jazz.

It was quite a gamble. They were playing live to a Nepali audience not familiar with the jazz territory. Would live improvisation work? “But the audience soon became intrigued even though they did not understand it initially,” he says. “Jazz is lively, and the energy of the music is contagious. People would give us cassettes of John Coltrane or Billie Holiday and tell us that our music reminded them of these artists. So really, it was the audience that introduced us to this unique jazz-funk sound that we are known for.”

As long lines of eager fans started filling the Jazz Upstairs bar, Cadenza expanded to doing live performances every Wednesday and Saturday. Chhetri says even after all these years, the bar feels like home.

Many listeners may notice that Cadenza’s music has a one-of-a-kind signature style due to genre fusion. Jazz instruments like saxophone, guitar, drums, and Afro-funk grooves with traditional Nepali folk rhythms and classical sounds such as damphu rhythms, Tamang selo, and bamboo flute.

MELTING POT

“Music is a language, once you understand the rules, you can write any story,” explains Chhetri. “Jazz is a melting pot for music and has always welcomed fusion, so blending Afrobeat and jazz with Nepali folk and Eastern classical didn’t feel unnatural or difficult. It felt authentic.”

As band members changed, collaborative projects expanded, and international musicians joined the fusion work. So, the name evolved into the present Cadenza Collective. Its performance at the Palmer Street Jazz Festival in Australia in 2001 was a milestone. Navin Chettri was inspired by it, and teamed up with Chhedup Bomzan of Jazz Upstairs Bar to establish Jazzmandu in 2002. It is now an annual musical festival that is celebrated with high regard (left).

“The long-lasting partnership and trust we received from Nepali Times and The Himalayan Times since the very first jazz festival, and Surya Nepal’s collaboration, made the festival possible. Jazzmandu couldn’t have grown to such a large scale without that support,” Chettri says.

Kathmandu’s live music landscape has come a long way. People were not used to paying to enter the bar, but Cadenza’s early collaborator Susan Sellers gave guests the choice to pay on the way out. Most did.

“I am very happy to see that musical literacy has made major strides in Nepal. I would even go so far as to say that the present is the golden time of music in Nepal,” Chhetri says.

Cadenza is performing its popular album ‘Back to the Roots’ at The Garden Project on Friday 24 October, and will also play in the upcoming Jazzmandu Festival.
